opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a bit of a myth that you need to have everything figured out before you start. Honestly, when I decided to start a company, I didn't have much experience running a business at all. My background was in research, in computer graphics and programming languages, building tools like Taichi. I knew how to write code and publish papers, but hiring, fundraising, managing people, building a product that customers actually pay for? Those were all new to me.

The way I see it, some things you simply can't learn without doing them. You can read all the books about startups and listen to all the advice, but until you're in it and you have to make a decision with incomplete information and real consequences, you don't really understand it. So at some point, thinking more stops being useful. You've reached the limit of what thinking can tell you, and the only way to get more information is to act.

That doesn't mean you should be reckless. I tried to think clearly about a few key questions. Is there a real problem here that I care deeply about? Do I have some unique advantage, maybe a technology or an insight or a community, that makes me a reasonable person to work on it? And what's the worst case? For me, the worst case was that it doesn't work out, I've learned a huge amount, and I can still go back to research or join another company. When you frame it like that, the downside is quite bounded, while the upside, in both impact and personal growth, is very large.

Timing also matters. When you're young, you have fewer obligations and more energy, and your opportunity cost is relatively low. If you wait until you feel fully ready, you might never go, because there's always one more thing to learn, and meanwhile your life gets more complicated.

So my view is: think enough to make sure the direction is meaningful and the risk is something you can live with, then jump in and be prepared to learn very fast. You will make mistakes. I certainly made plenty. But those mistakes are exactly how you gain the experience you didn't have at the start.

r001.rationale: The response says to act, make mistakes, and learn quickly, but does not clearly present rapid experimentation while building the company as the way to gain missing experience.

r002.rationale: It describes failure as a bounded downside because the founder could return to research or join another company, then advises starting when the risk is bearable even without feeling fully ready.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a three-and-a-half-year PhD, a two-year entrepreneurial attempt, or the equivalent five-and-a-half-year time cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think anyone has fully thought it through before they start. If you wait until you have, you probably never start.

For me, the honest answer is that I didn't take some big deliberate step. I was working on Taichi as a research project at MIT, and it was open source, and people started using it. Companies started emailing me asking how to do things with it. At some point the question kind of answered itself: there was demand, there was a community, and nobody else was going to build the thing around it. So the "decision" was less a leap and more just the next step that made sense.

That said, I want to be careful not to romanticize it. I was very inexperienced. I had no idea how to hire, how to manage, how to talk to investors. I made a lot of mistakes that an experienced founder wouldn't have made. But I think the key insight is that experience in running a company is mostly only obtainable by running a company. You can read books, you can talk to people, and I'd recommend doing both, but there's a kind of knowledge that only comes from making the mistakes yourself.

So my framework is roughly: don't ask "am I ready?" because the answer is always no. Ask "is there something real here that I care enough about to keep going when it gets hard?" If there's genuine demand and you have some unfair advantage, usually deep technical understanding of the problem, that's enough to start. Everything else you learn on the way.

And one more thing. The downside of trying when you're young is actually pretty small. If it fails, you learned a lot and you can go get a job. The downside of not trying is that you spend years wondering. I'd rather have the data.

r001.rationale: The response says company-running knowledge comes from running a company and learning from mistakes, but does not present rapid experimentation as the way to gain that experience.

r002.rationale: It says that if the venture fails, the founder can learn a lot and get a job, and presents the downside of trying while young as small enough to favor starting despite not feeling ready.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison involving a two-year failure, a three-and-a-half-year PhD, or an equivalent five-and-a-half-year time cost.

astra-6.text:
I think you don’t need to have everything figured out before you start. Of course, you should think carefully about what problem you want to solve and why it matters. But some questions you can only answer by actually doing the work—building something, talking to users, and seeing whether it helps them.

If you don’t have much experience, you can start with a small experiment. Can you make something useful for one person? Will they keep using it? That gives you a much better basis for the next decision than just thinking about starting a company in the abstract.

So I would treat it as a learning process. You need enough conviction to take the first step, but also enough flexibility to change your mind when you learn something new.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with a small experiment and learn by building and talking to users, presenting this as a way to gain a better basis for decisions despite limited experience.

r002.rationale: It encourages taking a first step with conviction and flexibility, but does not say that being able to bear the consequences of failure is sufficient reason to start.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a PhD, the stated durations, or compare the time cost of failure with completing the PhD.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to accept that you won’t have everything figured out before you start. There are things you can only learn by doing—talking to customers, building something, and seeing whether people actually need it. If you wait until you feel completely ready, you might wait forever.

That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t think carefully. I would focus on a few questions: Is this a problem I really care about? Do I have something useful to contribute? And am I willing to spend the next several years working on it? You don’t need a perfect plan, but you need a reason to keep going when your first plan turns out to be wrong.

r001.rationale: It says founders learn by talking to customers and building, but does not clearly present rapid experimentation as a way to gain initially lacking experience.

r002.rationale: It does not say that being able to bear failure’s consequences is sufficient reason to start before feeling prepared.

r003.rationale: It gives no comparison between a failed two-year venture after a three-and-a-half-year PhD and taking five and a half years to complete the PhD.
